content: Antipsychotic medications are the cornerstone of treatment for schizophrenia. Clinical guidelines suggest that there is no significant difference in efficacy among antipsychotic drugs. However, low-potency antipsychotics are often perceived in clinical practice as being less effective than high-potency drugs like haloperidol. Additionally, these two classes of drugs appear to differ in their side effect profiles. The objective of this review was to evaluate the clinical effects of haloperidol compared to low-potency first-generation antipsychotics in individuals with schizophrenia. A systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Schizophrenia Group Trials Register as of July 2010. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing haloperidol with low-potency first-generation antipsychotics in patients with schizophrenia or schizophrenia-like psychosis were included. Data were independently extracted, and statistical analyses were performed using a random-effects model. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, while mean differences (MD) were calculated for continuous outcomes. The review included 17 randomized trials with a total of 877 participants. The sample sizes of the studies ranged from 16 to 109 participants, and all studies were of short duration, lasting between two and 12 weeks. Reporting of key methodological aspects, such as sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding, was generally poor. There was no clear evidence to suggest that haloperidol was superior to low-potency antipsychotics in terms of clinical response. Specifically, 40% of participants in the haloperidol group and 36% in the low-potency antipsychotic group showed a clinical response (14 RCTs, n = 574, RR 1.11, CI 0.86 to 1.44; low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in treatment acceptability, as measured by the proportion of participants who discontinued the studies for any reason (haloperidol 13%, low-potency antipsychotics 17%, 11 RCTs, n = 408, RR 0.82, CI 0.38 to 1.77; low-quality evidence). Adverse effects were reported with varying frequencies between the two groups. Participants in the haloperidol group were more likely to experience movement disorders compared to those in the low-potency antipsychotic group (haloperidol 72%, low-potency antipsychotics 41%, 5 RCTs, n = 170, RR 1.64, CI 1.22 to 2.21; low-quality evidence). Conversely, participants in the low-potency antipsychotic group were more likely to experience sedation (haloperidol 14%, low-potency antipsychotics 41%, 2 RCTs, n = 44, RR 0.30, CI 0.11 to 0.82; moderate-quality evidence), orthostatic hypotension (haloperidol 25%, low-potency antipsychotics 71%, 1 RCT, n = 41, RR 0.35, CI 0.16 to 0.78), and weight gain (haloperidol 5%, low-potency antipsychotics 29%, 3 RCTs, n = 88, RR 0.22, CI 0.06 to 0.81). No data were available regarding mortality or quality of life outcomes. The primary outcome results were consistent across subgroup and sensitivity analyses. In conclusion, the evidence does not clearly demonstrate that haloperidol is more effective than low-potency antipsychotics for treating schizophrenia. Differences in adverse event profiles were observed, with movement disorders being more common in the haloperidol group, while sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and weight gain were more frequent in the low-potency antipsychotic group. The overall quality of the included studies was low, and the quality of evidence for the main outcomes ranged from moderate to very low. Further high-quality research is needed to determine whether haloperidol is superior or inferior to low-potency antipsychotics.
